title: The Gang Inflates

jokes.text: Mac unprompted defends Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles movies as 'more well-refined' while shopping for couches
jokes.setup: Two guys are casually shopping for couches in what seems like a normal scene
jokes.punchline: Mac is passionately evangelizing TMNT movies as 'well-refined' cinema with zero irony
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac stupidity — he uses sophisticated vocabulary ('well-refined') to describe a children's franchise. Works as character establishment but isn't exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You spent close to $20,000 on a couch you never owned.

jokes.text: It's revealed Mac and Dennis rented a couch for 15 years at $25/week — Dennis calculates they spent $19,500 on something they never owned
jokes.setup: Frank asks how much the interest on the rented couch was; Mac/Dennis say it was 'nothing, like 25 bucks a week'
jokes.punchline: Frank does the math live: 52 weeks x $25 x 15 years = $19,500. Mac and Dennis both say 'That seems high' as if doubting the math rather than their own stupidity
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured escalating reveal. The math is done in real-time for the audience (excellent structure). The characters' response — 'That seems high' — is the ideal punchline because they're questioning Frank's arithmetic rather than their own catastrophic financial decision. Strong character integration: only these two idiots could have done this for 15 years without noticing.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That seems high.

jokes.text: Frank's rapid-fire math: 52 weeks × $25 × 15 years = $19,500
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis insist the interest on their rented couch was 'nothing'
jokes.punchline: Frank calmly and instantly does the math to reveal they spent nearly $20,000 on a couch they never owned
jokes.explanation: Frank's flat, matter-of-fact delivery of devastating arithmetic is very funny. The economy is excellent — three numbers, one pause, maximum damage. Character-consistent: Frank as the cynical financial shark.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I have glued my hand to the door, so they can't physically remove me.

jokes.text: 'That's pretty bad business, fellas.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just calculated they spent $19,500 on a couch they never owned
jokes.punchline: Frank's clinical understatement — 'That's pretty bad business, fellas' — delivered with total calm
jokes.explanation: Frank's deadpan understatement is a reliable comedic tool here. 'Pretty bad' for a $19,500 couch rental is hilariously understated. Economy is strong — fewer words say more.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Charlie, we don't want to hear it.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis enthusiastically explain inflation while Dee is on the phone in crisis, repeatedly talking over her
jokes.setup: Dee calls to say she's being evicted and has glued her hand to a door; the gang briefly acknowledges her then immediately cuts back to the economics lesson
jokes.punchline: 'Just a second, Deandra' — they literally pause Dee mid-crisis to hear Frank explain inflation
jokes.explanation: Perfect encapsulation of the gang's cruelty and self-absorption. Dee's crisis is literally dismissed mid-sentence so they can hear an economics lecture. Very character-integrated — the gang has ALWAYS treated Dee as a non-entity.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: So maybe what we would need to do is lower our wages. I get it.

jokes.text: Charlie insists he knows business from 'living with Frank' and asks to pitch an investment idea, only to be immediately shut down
jokes.setup: Charlie claims expertise from proximity to Frank; tries to pitch his idea
jokes.punchline: 'Charlie, we don't want to hear it. Frank, keep going.' — Charlie is dismissed before he can even start
jokes.explanation: Setup for a running gag throughout the episode (Charlie pitching his crypto idea). First instance is functional but unremarkable.

dialogue.line: That's money talk.

jokes.text: Frank explains that raising wages causes inflation, then suggests lowering wages would cause a recession and depression — the gang agrees they can't take a pay cut OR a raise, then concludes 'That's money talk'
jokes.setup: Mac asks if prices going up means they can get a raise; Frank explains this would increase inflation
jokes.punchline: They all solemnly agree they cannot get raises OR pay cuts, arriving at complete paralysis, and declare 'That's money talk' with great pride
jokes.explanation: The joke is that they've arrived at a totally useless conclusion — no raise, no cut, do nothing — and they're proud of understanding it. 'That's money talk' becomes a recurring catchphrase that earns its first laugh here.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: But I'll give you 50 cents for a buck.

jokes.text: Frank's extended metaphor about 'nut' — asking how much nut they go through, whether they're storing their nut or blowing through it
jokes.setup: Frank tries to explain personal finance using 'nut' as slang for money/savings
jokes.punchline: The repeated use of 'nut' — 'how much nut do you blow through,' 'you got to try to hang on to some of that nut' — has an increasingly double-meaning quality that the characters accept completely straight
jokes.explanation: Frank using 'nut' as financial slang while everyone accepts it completely straight is a sustained wordplay gag. The word recurs throughout the episode in increasingly absurd contexts (Fancy Nuts, eating nuts in bed). Strong quotability.

dialogue.line: An inflatable couch?

jokes.text: 'Yeah, but I'll give you 50 cents for a buck.' / 'Hey. Uh, I think that sounds like a good deal.'
jokes.setup: Frank explains a dollar is only worth 25 cents due to inflation
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately offers to give Frank 50 cents for a dollar — thinking he's making a smart deal — and Dennis agrees it sounds good
jokes.explanation: Sharp comedic moment. Mac hears that a dollar is worth 25 cents and immediately tries to exploit that by offering 50 cents — still a rip-off for him — and Dennis endorses it. Perfect demonstration of their confident stupidity. The logic is internally consistent while being completely wrong, which is the hallmark of good gang idiocy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: These are very fancy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Are they? Three dollars?

jokes.text: The gang's economics lesson concludes: can't raise wages (inflation), can't cut wages (recession/depression), so nothing can change — 'That's money talk'
jokes.setup: Frank explains why raising wages would cause inflation and cutting wages would cause a recession
jokes.punchline: The gang nods sagely, concluding with 'That's money talk' — having learned they're completely trapped and nothing can be done
jokes.explanation: 'That's money talk' as the gang's catchphrase for financial nihilism is a good running gag seed. The joke captures how economic discussion often leads to paralysis while sounding authoritative. 'That's money talk' earns its quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, well, you can't inflate this any further 'cause it'll pop.

jokes.text: Frank exchanges a ten for a five from Dennis while Dee is screaming for help on the phone
jokes.setup: Dee is screaming on the phone about being evicted and needing Frank's wire transfer
jokes.punchline: Frank quietly tells Dennis 'I only have a ten, I'll give you a five' — completing their money-is-not-worth-face-value transaction while ignoring Dee's crisis entirely
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Dee's screaming desperation with Frank's calm money transaction is a good cringe beat. The 'That's money talk' callback punctuates it well.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I just kept blowing and blowing and blowing, and just... boom.

jokes.text: Frank exchanges a ten for a five, says 'That's money talk. Let's go.' Everyone agrees
jokes.setup: The economics discussion has gone full circle into absurdity
jokes.punchline: Frank trades a ten for a five and everyone celebrates it as 'money talk' and a done deal
jokes.explanation: Second use of 'money talk' — the running gag is building. The specificity of Frank trading a ten for a five and treating it as a business triumph is a good button on the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You mean to tell me we've been living here all this time, and you never told me we had a bathroom?

jokes.text: Mac 'basically lives on' Dwayne Johnson energy drinks and Dennis tells him he doesn't have to buy everything The Rock tries to sell him
jokes.setup: Dennis is reviewing their budget and asks about Mac's spending
jokes.punchline: Mac has fully surrendered his purchasing autonomy to whatever Dwayne Johnson endorses
jokes.explanation: Very Mac — his gym-bro hero worship extends to literal brand discipleship. Quick, clean character joke. Not exceptional but well-placed.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: We piss in cans, Charlie.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis are sitting on a visibly cheap inflatable couch in their apartment — the visual reveal
jokes.setup: Mac tells Dennis to 'come have a seat' with excitement
jokes.punchline: The camera reveals a sad inflatable couch as their replacement for the $19,500 rented sofa — accompanied by audible squeaking
jokes.explanation: The visual gag earns well because of the setup — they just learned they wasted $19,500 on a couch, and their solution is an inflatable pool toy. The squeak is a nice textural addition. Good economy — the image does the comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I wasn't trying to be crypto about it, it's just, like, Frank, I just never liked sleeping in a room with an empty room behind me.

jokes.text: 'We own it. Dennis, we own it.' — Mac proudly announces they own the inflatable couch
jokes.setup: Mac explains the inflatable couch lowers their monthly 'nut' because they're not renting it
jokes.punchline: He announces ownership of a $20 pool toy with the pride of a man who just paid off a mortgage
jokes.explanation: The callback to the couch-rental disaster makes this land harder. Mac's pride is proportional to the magnitude of their previous failure, which is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I don't want to live in a maze, you know?

jokes.text: Mac produces a giant bulk tin of 'Fancy Nuts' as a cost-saving measure
jokes.setup: Mac says he also bought something to lower costs
jokes.punchline: He pulls out what are clearly cheap dollar-store nuts marketed as 'Fancy' — only $3
jokes.explanation: The 'Fancy Nuts' prop is introduced here and pays off repeatedly throughout the episode. The setup of Mac calling them fancy while Dennis dismisses them as 'low-end economy nuts' is a solid bit. The nuts become a recurring comedic object.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm gonna have to get a butler.

jokes.text: Dennis says he wants to 'inflate things a little further'; Mac warns you can't inflate the couch more or it'll pop; Dennis: 'Just a figure of speech'; Mac: 'No, trust me, I tried. I already popped two of them earlier today.'
jokes.setup: Dennis uses 'inflate' metaphorically to describe their business plan
jokes.punchline: Mac has literally been inflating the couch and already popped two of them — he missed the metaphor entirely and also wasted their furniture stock
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac literal-mindedness. The wordplay between literal and figurative inflation is elegant and the reveal that he's already destroyed their product is a great escalation. The episode's title 'The Gang Inflates' gains resonance here.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Wait, so you truly have no reason to be sleeping with Frank.

jokes.text: 'I just kept blowing and blowing and blowing, and just... boom.' / 'You really shouldn't, it's dangerous. I'm serious, Dennis. Don't blow this up.'
jokes.setup: Mac explains he already popped two couches from over-inflation
jokes.punchline: Dennis warns 'Don't blow this up' — simultaneously a literal instruction about the couch AND a figurative warning about their business plan, delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: The double meaning works well and Dennis's straight delivery of a dual-meaning warning is well-executed. Good economy — the line does double duty.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Charlie, you mean we've been living in a two-bedroom with a bathroom, and you never said anything about it?

jokes.text: Charlie keeps coming home with lamps — 'That's like the fifth lamp you've brought back'
jokes.setup: Charlie enters with what appears to be a new lamp
jokes.punchline: Frank reveals this is part of a pattern — Charlie keeps acquiring lamps for no apparent reason
jokes.explanation: Very Charlie — inexplicable acquisitions with no explanation. The lamps pay off later in the episode when Frank grabs them while robbing tenants. Good setup for a later payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's a lot of blowing.

jokes.text: Charlie pitches crypto and uses 'cryptic' as a malapropism: 'it'd be a lot less cryptic if I could show you the video'
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to pitch Frank on crypto investment
jokes.punchline: He uses 'cryptic' instead of a real explanation, apparently not fully understanding the word 'crypto' either
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie verbal comedy — the near-miss on 'crypto/cryptic' perfectly captures his half-educated attempts at business speak. Very character-specific. This is exactly the kind of inadvertent wordplay Charlie does, and it works as setup for the callback at episode's end ('you kept it crypto').

dialogue.line: What happened to your lips?

jokes.text: Frank discovers there's a toilet in Charlie and Frank's apartment — 'We piss in cans, Charlie.'
jokes.setup: Frank finds what appears to be a bathroom in their apartment
jokes.punchline: 'We piss in cans, Charlie' — said with genuine indignation, as if the toilet is the aberration
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The joke inverts normal outrage — Frank is upset not that they've been using cans when a toilet existed, but that Charlie has been hiding the toilet from their established can-pissing lifestyle. 'We piss in cans' as a statement of identity and lifestyle is deeply character-specific and instantly quotable. The economy is perfect — four words establish a whole world of degradation. This approaches the 8-anchor quality.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That is rancid.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Did you get a bad one?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Well, they're all bad.

jokes.text: Charlie's explanation for hiding the bedroom: 'I just never liked sleeping in a room with an empty room behind me. It's creepy.'
jokes.setup: Frank discovers there's been a second bedroom this whole time while Charlie slept with Frank
jokes.punchline: Charlie's justification is not greed or laziness but a phobia about empty rooms — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. The reveal that Charlie has been willingly sleeping in the same bed/room as Frank when a whole extra room was available is absurd enough. But his justification — a fear of empty rooms — is so bizarre, so internally consistent with Charlie's psychology, and so completely unexplained that it becomes the joke. Only Charlie would have this specific anxiety. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Kim Kardashian's backside, the early years.

jokes.text: Frank complains about having to walk across the apartment to answer the door: 'I'm going to have to walk a mile to get it' / 'I'm gonna have to get a butler'
jokes.setup: Frank discovers his apartment is actually a large two-bedroom with a bathroom
jokes.punchline: Frank treats walking across his own apartment as an extraordinary hardship requiring staff
jokes.explanation: Decent Frank joke. His dramatic reaction to basic apartment-dwelling is in character. Somewhat predictable rich-man-in-poor-circumstances beat, but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: The Kardashians' net worth has inflated in direct proportion to their booties.

jokes.text: The gang discovers the extra room one by one — each person's 'Holy shit' reaction upon seeing it, repeated as a running gag
jokes.setup: Frank finds the room; then Mac and Dennis arrive and find it; then Dee finds it
jokes.punchline: Each successive 'Holy shit' at the same room is funnier because the room itself is entirely normal — the joke is everyone's disbelief at Charlie's lifestyle choice
jokes.explanation: The repeated revelation structure works well. Each new 'Holy shit' recontextualizes Charlie's choice. The cumulative effect is good. Not one knockout punch but sustained comedic momentum.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm in.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You're in? You don't need to hear the whole pitch?

jokes.text: 'Wait, so you truly have no reason to be sleeping with Frank.' / 'Move past it, dude. Move past it, man.'
jokes.setup: Mac sees the extra bedroom and realizes Charlie has been voluntarily sleeping with Frank
jokes.punchline: Mac's clinical observation cuts to the heart of Charlie's arrangement; Charlie deflects with 'move past it' rather than engaging with the obvious conclusion
jokes.explanation: Sharp and dark. The implication about Charlie and Frank's sleeping arrangement is a long-running show joke, and 'you truly have no reason to be sleeping with Frank' landing like a logical observation rather than an accusation is very funny. Charlie's desperate 'move past it' is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: People are doing it to call attention to injustices or some shit. I don't know. Either way, I'm locked in.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis kick Charlie and Dee out so they can use the room as 'the office' — Charlie: 'Oh, now it's an office? Are we even zoned for that?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis claim Frank's newly discovered room for a business meeting
jokes.punchline: Charlie sarcastically protests being kicked out of a room in his own apartment, then zoning laws become the specific grievance
jokes.explanation: Solid but not exceptional. The zoning grievance is a funny specific detail. Charlie complaining about process rather than the actual absurdity of the situation is characterful.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He's jacking off into a magazine.

jokes.text: Mac's lips are visibly swollen/damaged from blowing up the plastic inflatable furniture — Frank asks 'What happened to your lips?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have been blowing up inflatable furniture all morning in preparation for the pitch
jokes.punchline: Mac's lips are grotesquely damaged; he insists it's from 'the plastic' rather than the obvious answer (he blew up too many couches)
jokes.explanation: Visual payoff to the earlier blowing gag. Mac's physical deterioration from his job is a nice running element. The escalation of his physical symptoms throughout the episode is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm not investing in them because I believe in them. I'm investing in them because I don't believe in them.

jokes.text: Mac offers Frank a 'Fancy Nut' to open the meeting; Frank bites one and declares 'That is rancid. Do not eat them. Either of you.'
jokes.setup: Mac presents the Fancy Nuts with great ceremony as part of the professional pitch
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately spits it out and bans both of them from eating the nuts they were planning to 'live on for weeks'
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the Fancy Nuts setup. Frank's immediate rejection and his authority in banning the nuts is funny. The fact that their primary cost-saving food measure is inedible is a nice escalation of their incompetence.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's your goddamn wheezing.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Am I wheezing?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Are you wheezing? You sound insane.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis present a lookbook for their inflatable furniture business that opens with Kim Kardashian's backside — 'The early years'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are pitching their inflatable furniture business to Frank using a lookbook
jokes.punchline: The business pitch begins with Kim Kardashian's butt photos labeled 'the early years'
jokes.explanation: The pivot from professional pitch to Kardashian butt photos is a great subversion of business presentation norms. The 'early years' labeling implies they have a full portfolio of her posterior evolution. Genuinely surprising and committed to the bit.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You ever have a pine nut? Which one is... A fancy tree?

jokes.text: Frank immediately agrees to invest without hearing the full pitch: 'I'm in. You-you don't need to hear the whole pitch?' / 'Nah.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have been building to a comprehensive pitch; we expect negotiation
jokes.punchline: Frank commits before they even finish — subverting the expected pitch format entirely
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — the pitch format is subverted. The payoff (Frank already knows they'll fail) recontextualizes his easy agreement, adding a layer of dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Frank's not the only one who can be a predatory lender. I say we pivot.

jokes.text: Frank wants to keep 'the book' for 'other reasons' — the Kardashian lookbook is now Frank's personal property
jokes.setup: Frank agrees to the loan terms and negotiates keeping the inflatable furniture
jokes.punchline: He also wants the Kardashian lookbook, delivered with a knowing pause: 'other reasons'
jokes.explanation: Frank's 'other reasons' is perfectly economical. The implied use of the book is disgusting and completely in character. The characters' knowing 'yeah, we figured you'd want to...' suggests they built the pitch around Frank's appetites. Good dark character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Go for it, bitch! We got bulletproof vests on!

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, no, I don't. I don't have a bulletproof vest.

jokes.text: FYI — Frank does not want to be bothered because 'he's jacking off into a magazine' — said matter-of-factly
jokes.setup: Charlie asks why Frank can't be disturbed; Dennis explains with complete nonchalance
jokes.punchline: 'He's jacking off into a magazine. Right.' Delivered as if this is a perfectly normal workplace status update
jokes.explanation: The payoff on Frank's 'other reasons' for the lookbook arrives almost immediately and is delivered by Dennis with the same matter-of-fact tone as a meeting update. 'He's jacking off into a magazine' as a reason a colleague is unavailable is very Frank and very Always Sunny. Strong economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What? You're my landlord?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah, I got tired of paying your rent all those years, so I bought the building.

jokes.text: Dennis asks 'He's making homophobic jokes for the...' about Mac's lip situation; Mac cuts him off: 'Not homophobic.'
jokes.setup: Frank asked about Mac's lips; Dennis and Mac are explaining the blowing context
jokes.punchline: Dennis identifies that the 'blowing' jokes are going in a homophobic direction; Mac's flat denial is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Meta-aware moment about the show's own comedic tendencies. Dennis calling out the homophobic joke trajectory while Mac defensively denies it references the show's long-running engagement with Mac's sexuality. The joke works on two levels — within the scene and as self-commentary.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: I don't have a pool, so...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, no, no, no, I see, I see the confusion. No, we're talking about for inside.

jokes.text: Frank reveals he only invested because he doesn't believe in them — 'I'm investing in them because I don't believe in them. They're gonna be paying me money for the rest of their lives, like that stupid couch.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is upset Frank chose Mac and Dennis's idea; Frank explains his reasoning
jokes.punchline: Frank's investment is a predatory scheme based on certainty of their failure — the couch rental is explicitly invoked as the template
jokes.explanation: This is a great structural joke. The episode's inciting premise (they wasted $19,500 on a couch they rented) becomes the blueprint for Frank's deliberate predation. The callback gives the earlier joke new meaning retroactively. 'Like that stupid couch' is an elegant call-back anchor. Frank's inversion of investment logic (he invests in failure) is both darkly funny and consistent with his character.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You pay full price for your couch? That's outrageous.

jokes.text: Dee is still glued to Charlie's door — 'I'm still here, goddamn it.' Charlie offers to 'glue a pillow to the wall' as hospitality: 'I don't want to be a bad host.'
jokes.setup: Charlie refuses to unglue Dee but acknowledges she needs to use the new bathroom
jokes.punchline: Charlie offering to glue a pillow to the wall for comfort is treated as genuine hospitality
jokes.explanation: Charlie's twisted logic — he won't free her but wants to make her comfortable while captive — is very Charlie. 'I don't want to be a bad host' while leaving someone glued to a wall is perfect character comedy. His hospitality instinct overriding his refusal to actually help her is a great small moment.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm making a bet that the SEC's not gonna regulate. Of course, regulation's gonna come in at some point, it always does, but right now it's completely unregulated.

jokes.text: Mac is wheezing loudly from the nuts; Dennis can hear it in the dark: 'Are you wheezing? You sound insane. Are you allergic to those nuts?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are trying to sleep; Dennis is kept awake
jokes.punchline: Mac is making alarming sounds from an apparent allergic reaction, still denying it's the nuts
jokes.explanation: Functional escalation of the nut subplot. Mac insisting it's not the nuts while clearly suffering from the nuts is a standard comedic beat, but it's well-integrated with the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Charlie, did you take all of my money and invest it in a box full of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle Pies?

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Also, I feel like I'm sleeping in a tub of nuts here, man. Can you stop eating them in bed?'
jokes.setup: Dennis is already annoyed by Mac's wheezing
jokes.punchline: Mac has been eating the rancid Fancy Nuts in bed, apparently filling the bed with them
jokes.explanation: 'I'm sleeping in a tub of nuts' is a funny image — Mac has been eating the declared-rancid nuts in bed despite Frank's prohibition. The escalation of the nut consequences (swollen lips → wheezing → sleeping in a nut tub) is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Charlie, did you take all of my money and invest it in a box full of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle Pies?

jokes.text: Mac claims he's not allergic to the nuts — 'It's not the nuts. I think it's from blowing up those...' — Dennis: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Mac is visibly having an allergic reaction
jokes.punchline: Mac insists it's from the plastic on the inflatables; Dennis's flat 'No' shuts it down
jokes.explanation: Mac's denial is consistent with the episode's through-line. Dennis's economy — just 'No' — is the best possible response. Good but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Are they made from real turtle?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Probably.

jokes.text: Charlie arrives for housing, then produces his 'own nuts' — Dennis: 'Are they fancy?' / Charlie: 'What?' / Mac: 'Are they Fancy Nuts?' / 'Well, some are, yeah. It's an assortment.'
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to negotiate a place to stay by offering his own nuts as a contribution
jokes.punchline: The only quality standard that matters is whether they're Fancy — and Charlie's assortment meets partial criteria
jokes.explanation: The Fancy Nuts have fully taken on a ritualistic importance — they're now the apartment's de facto currency. The sequence where both Mac and Dennis independently confirm the 'fancy' requirement is funny escalation. 'It's an assortment' is a perfect Charlie answer.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: 'Cause I bought the last remaining ones there are.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: No... Nice work.

jokes.text: Charlie arrives at Mac and Dennis's needing a place to stay — 'I'll inflate it, I'll deflate it. It'll be like I was never here. Plus, I brought my own nuts.'
jokes.setup: Charlie shows up needing a place to stay; Mac and Dennis say there's no room
jokes.punchline: Charlie offers to inflate/deflate his own bed each day as evidence of minimal impact, then seals the deal with 'Plus, I brought my own nuts'
jokes.explanation: Charlie's 'offering' escalation — inflate/deflate + own nuts — is perfectly Charlie. The nuts callback lands well. 'Plus, I brought my own nuts' as the clinching argument is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That's inflation, Frank.

jokes.text: 'Consider it an offering.' Dennis: 'Of war?' Charlie: 'Of peace. What is going on with you, dude?'
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to present the nuts as a gift to earn his stay
jokes.punchline: Dennis interprets 'offering' as an act of aggression; Charlie's bewildered 'What is going on with you, dude?' acknowledges Dennis's hostility without understanding it
jokes.explanation: 'Of war?' is a great Dennis line — paranoid, confrontational, out of proportion. The exchange is tight and fast. 'What is going on with you, dude?' is a good reaction that implicitly acknowledges Dennis's psychological instability. High economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Are you still eating the nuts?

jokes.text: Charlie demands to be cut in on the business as payment for his information — 'See? I am a pretty good businessman after all.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has information about Frank's predatory lending; he negotiates before revealing it
jokes.punchline: Charlie congratulates himself on his business acumen for executing a simple bribe
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Charlie's frustrated attempts to be taken seriously as a businessman. His pride in executing a basic quid pro quo is characterful, though not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I think we'll take you to the hospital, and they'll have nuts, and you can die there.

jokes.text: Dennis calls out Charlie for 'bartering with nuts that you probably foraged from a tree'
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to negotiate with his nuts
jokes.punchline: Dennis identifies that Charlie likely gathered the nuts himself from a tree — a very feral Charlie behavior delivered as a pointed accusation
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie observation. The image of Charlie foraging nuts from a tree and presenting them as currency in a business negotiation is completely plausible within the show's world, which is what makes it funny. Dennis's matter-of-fact accusation lands well.

jokes.text: 'A fancy tree? One of the fanciest, Mac. Which one?' — The Fancy Nuts negotiation continues
jokes.setup: Dennis has accused Charlie of foraging his nuts; Mac follows up asking which fancy tree
jokes.punchline: Mac is completely sincere in asking which tree, treating tree-fanciness as a real quality standard; Charlie answers 'one of the fanciest'
jokes.explanation: The 'fancy tree' exchange is the peak of the Fancy Nuts running gag. Mac's sincere inquiry and Charlie's self-important 'one of the fanciest' is absurdist comedy done right. The word 'fancy' has been completely divorced from meaning by this point.

jokes.text: 'You ever have a pine nut?'
jokes.setup: Mac asks which fancy tree; Charlie builds anticipation
jokes.punchline: The grand reveal is a pine nut — the most common, cheapest nut — delivered with the gravity of a sommelier revealing a vintage
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words do enormous work. The setup (which fancy tree?) builds expectation; 'you ever have a pine nut?' deflates it completely while Charlie treats it as a revelation. The beat between Mac's 'which one?' and Charlie's answer is timed to maximize the mundane reveal. This is one of the best moments in the episode — it's the perfect anti-climax delivered with maximum confidence.

jokes.text: Charlie's crypto pitch is revealed — he wants them to pool their nut, make 'a huge pile of green,' and 'everyone gets a taste' and 'slurping that shit down'
jokes.setup: Dee and Charlie claim to have information and a business solution; they pitch pooling their money
jokes.punchline: Charlie's financial metaphors collapse into imagery of physically consuming piles of green, which confuses everyone
jokes.explanation: Charlie's money-talk breaking down into physical food metaphors ('slurping that shit down') is characteristically Charlie. Dennis: 'I didn't love the sound of that' and Charlie clarifying with 'like a huge pile of green...everyone is slurping that shit down' is funny because Charlie's clarification makes it worse.

jokes.text: Dennis's pivot: 'Frank's not the only one who can be a predatory lender. I say we rent them the inflatables'
jokes.setup: The gang discovers Frank is predatorily lending to them
jokes.punchline: Dennis's response to being scammed is to immediately become the same kind of scammer — renting inflatables instead of selling them, the same scheme as the couch
jokes.explanation: This is the structural centerpiece of the episode. Dennis's instant moral pivot — from victim to perpetrator of the exact same scheme — is the show's whole thesis about its characters. The callback to the couch rental (Joke 2) closes the loop perfectly. The gang will now do to customers what was done to them. It's dark, it's character-consistent, and structurally it's the most satisfying joke in the episode because it crystallizes the theme. Dennis doesn't even pause to reflect.

jokes.text: Dee's crypto pitch is played as confident 'money talk' but is completely garbled buzzword soup — 'over-leveraged,' 'speculative market,' 'SEC regulation,' 'getting out over our skis'
jokes.setup: Dee claims to have a solution to all their problems
jokes.punchline: Her pitch is entirely financial jargon strung together with no real meaning, delivered with supreme confidence
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Dee sounds competent while saying nothing coherent. 'That's money talk' from the gang validates her non-sense. This mirrors the opening scene's economics discussion — none of them actually understand finance but they all perform understanding.

jokes.text: Frank, armed and vested, robbing his own tenants while Dee watches — 'You're a slumlord now?' / 'Yes, I collect on these guys, and if they don't pay, I throw 'em out on the street, like I did you.'
jokes.setup: Dee realizes Frank has been her landlord the whole time
jokes.punchline: Frank casually confirms he's been her landlord, raised her rent, and had her evicted — his explanation is completely matter-of-fact
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural payoff. Dee's eviction crisis in scene one is revealed to be Frank's deliberate act. 'Like I did you' lands as a perfect dark punchline — the whole episode, Dee was screaming for help and Frank was her landlord the whole time. Strong Always Sunny cruelty.

jokes.text: 'That's money talk. Where did you learn to talk like that?' / 'Living with Frank, man.' — Charlie finally gets credit
jokes.setup: Dee and Charlie have delivered financial-sounding pitches
jokes.punchline: Charlie points out he's been saying all episode he learned business from Frank — now they're impressed by the same claim they dismissed earlier
jokes.explanation: Good structural callback. The same 'living with Frank' justification that got Charlie dismissed repeatedly now earns respect because Dee's buzzword pitch impressed them. The irony of the gang crediting Charlie only after someone else does the same thing is characterful.

jokes.text: 'Why did you raise the rent?' / 'Inflation. I got to increase my nut.' — Frank's justification for evicting Dee
jokes.setup: Dee confronts Frank about raising her rent
jokes.punchline: Frank uses the episode's economic lesson to justify evicting Dee, citing 'my nut' — the slang term that's been running all episode
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode callback. Everything comes full circle: the inflation conversation at the start, Frank's 'nut' economics lesson, and Dee's eviction are all connected in one line. 'Inflation. I got to increase my nut.' is concise, character-perfect, and ties together the episode's themes. Very high economy — five words crystallize the whole episode.

jokes.text: It's revealed that the investment Charlie's been pitching all episode is actually Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle Pies from 1991 — 'Now, Charlie, did you take all of my money and invest it in a box full of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle Pies?'
jokes.setup: All episode Charlie has been trying to pitch his 'Internet money kind of situation' / crypto investment
jokes.punchline: He spent their entire nut on a box of 1991 snack pies
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode and one of the stronger Always Sunny reveals. The structure is exceptional: (1) Mac mentions TMNT in the cold open, apparently randomly; (2) Charlie teases his investment idea throughout but is constantly shut down; (3) the reveal connects both threads. It rewards the audience for paying attention and makes the TMNT cold open retroactively meaningful. Only Charlie would sincerely believe vintage snack pies are a crypto-equivalent investment vehicle. Dennis's perfectly flat delivery of the reveal ('did you take all of my money and invest it in a box full of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle Pies') earns its own laugh. This is comparable to the 8.0 anchor and exceeds it in structural complexity.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I'm gonna blow our shoes out with all this walking' — complaining about the outdoor wind affecting their inflatable furniture display
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are running their inflatable furniture business outside; it's windy
jokes.punchline: Mac is worried about literally wearing out his shoes from walking in wind, treating it as a physical hazard
jokes.explanation: Minor moment, more transition than joke. The wind destroying their inflatable setup is a visual gag but the shoe line is fairly weak.

jokes.text: Tenant threatens to get his gun — Frank: 'Go for it, bitch! We got bulletproof vests on!' / Dee: 'Oh, no, I don't. I don't have a bulletproof vest.'
jokes.setup: Confronted by the tenant who threatens to get his gun
jokes.punchline: Frank taunts him with bulletproof vest claim; Dee's immediate correction reveals she has no vest and was not consulted about the plan
jokes.explanation: Very well-timed. Frank's bravado is immediately punctured by Dee's aside — she wasn't included in the bulletproof vest provision. The implication that Frank has a vest but didn't get one for Dee is classically cruel Frank. 'Oh, no, I don't. I don't have a bulletproof vest.' delivered as a corrective murmur while facing down a gun threat is excellent.

jokes.text: Charlie clarifies: 'I wasn't sure you knew what they were' — taking pride that Dennis recognized TMNT
jokes.setup: Dennis has just identified the Ninja Turtle Pies correctly
jokes.punchline: Charlie, in the middle of being confronted about wasting all their money, is pleased Dennis knew TMNT
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Charlie — his priorities are completely inverted. Being caught having wasted everyone's money is secondary to receiving validation that Dennis knows TMNT. The beat works because Charlie's sincerity is total. Good economy.

jokes.text: Dee discovers Frank is her landlord: 'What? You're my landlord?' / Frank: 'Yeah, I got tired of paying your rent all those years, so I bought the building.'
jokes.setup: Frank reveals he's the landlord who evicted Dee
jokes.punchline: He explains he bought the building specifically so he could stop paying her rent and then raise it
jokes.explanation: Perfect Frank and Dee dynamic joke. Frank's indifference to his daughter's housing security — he bought her building just to monetize it — is darkly funny and completely in character. The reveal is well-paced: Dee's shock, Frank's matter-of-fact explanation. The escalation that he then raised the rent to increase his 'nut' is the button.

jokes.text: Charlie proposes sitting on the pies — 'maybe eat one or two' — as an investment strategy
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis ask if they could quickly flip the pies for profit
jokes.punchline: Charlie's investment thesis includes the possibility of eating part of their investment, presented as a reasonable trade-off
jokes.explanation: Charlie's investor mindset encompasses consuming the investment. He genuinely sees 'eat one or two' as an acceptable cost within the asset management strategy. This is exactly the kind of thing that would only occur to Charlie.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis set up their inflatable furniture business outdoors — it's too windy and everything is blowing around
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are excited to launch their inflatable furniture business
jokes.punchline: The fundamental flaw in inflatable outdoor retail — wind — immediately becomes apparent; Dennis insists 'it's fine' despite everything blowing away
jokes.explanation: Decent visual comedy — inflatable furniture in the wind is a logical and funny problem. Dennis insisting 'it's fine' while stuff blows everywhere is good character work. Physical comedy that works better seen than described.

jokes.text: Frank arrives with a gun and a vest demanding loan repayment — Charlie: 'What do you got there?' Frank: '1991's delicious cream-filled Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle Pies, fresh from the sewers to me.'
jokes.setup: Frank arrives to collect on the loan with a gun and bulletproof vest
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately clocks the pies and identifies them specifically, including the 'fresh from the sewers' callback to the TMNT lore
jokes.explanation: 'Fresh from the sewers to me' is a great line — it acknowledges the TMNT mythology (turtles live in sewers) while Frank casually identifies the pies with the expertise of a man who knows his vintage snack foods. The armed loan collector arriving and pivoting immediately to pie knowledge is a funny tonal shift.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis's sales pitch accidentally implies the customer should be renting their couch: 'How much do you currently rent your couch for?' / 'I don't rent my couch.' / 'What? You pay full price for your couch?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are attempting to sell inflatable couches to a passerby
jokes.punchline: Their sales approach reveals they genuinely believe everyone rents their couch, and paying full price is the outrageous option
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. Their own financial catastrophe (renting a couch for $19,500) has completely distorted their market assumptions. They've built a business model around a behavior no normal person engages in. 'You pay full price for your couch?' as genuine shock is a perfect character beat — their stupidity has created a totally inverted worldview.

jokes.text: Dennis's customer pitch: 'What if I told you you could get your furniture for free?' — immediately followed by 'times are very inflatable right now'
jokes.setup: Dennis spots a customer and takes over the pitch
jokes.punchline: He confidently opens with 'free furniture' (which will mean paying interest forever) and then accidentally says 'inflatable' instead of 'inflationary' — total malapropism mid-pitch
jokes.explanation: 'Times are very inflatable right now' as a malapropism mid-sales pitch is funny — Dennis's confident salesmanship colliding with his actual confusion about the difference between 'inflation' and 'inflatable.' Mac's immediate 'stop, stop' is the right reaction. The pitch perfectly reenacts the predatory rental scam with the same opening lie.

jokes.text: Wind blows away all the inflatable furniture — 'Oh, shit.' / 'Oh, no.' — visual catastrophe
jokes.setup: Mac noted it was windy; they proceed anyway with the display of inflatable furniture
jokes.punchline: The wind destroys their entire inventory in a moment
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy payoff to the wind setup. Predictable but visually satisfying. The earlier wind warning makes this earned rather than cheap, but it's not a surprising joke.

jokes.text: Mac insists on going to Costco for more nuts rather than the hospital after losing all their furniture: 'Oh, and spend the remainder of our nut on medical bills? I don't think so, Dennis.'
jokes.setup: Mac is visibly ill from the nuts; Dennis tells him to go to the hospital
jokes.punchline: Mac prioritizes financial frugality over his apparent medical emergency, using the episode's economic framework to justify it
jokes.explanation: Mac applying their economic framework ('the nut') to a medical emergency is good character work. The word 'nut' in a medical context is an unexpected but earned application of the running gag.

jokes.text: The 'investment' is revealed: a box of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle Pies from 1991
jokes.setup: Everyone has pooled their money into Charlie's mysterious investment
jokes.punchline: The 'speculative market' investment is a cardboard box of TMNT Pies from 1991 — the same franchise Mac was evangelizing in scene one
jokes.explanation: The best structural moment in the episode. The cold open TMNT conversation — which seemed like disconnected small talk — was actually the seed of Charlie's entire investment thesis. The 'crypto' that Charlie kept pitching and everyone dismissed was TMNT Pies all along. The callback is elegant: it rewards attentive viewers, it's completely in character for Charlie (vintage collectible nostalgia as currency), and it recontextualizes the whole episode. This is excellent episode construction.

jokes.text: Frank arrives armed and vested to collect his loan — 'I'm armed and I got a vest, so don't try nothing'
jokes.setup: Frank interrupts the TMNT pie discussion
jokes.punchline: Frank's first installment collection is backed up by being armed and bulletproof-vested — mirroring the earlier robbery scene and confirming he runs all his financial dealings like organized crime
jokes.explanation: Frank arriving armed and vested for a first loan installment is a good character beat — his financial and criminal lives are completely merged. The vest callback is satisfying.

jokes.text: 'Are they made from real turtle?' / 'Probably.'
jokes.setup: Frank inspects the Ninja Turtle Pies
jokes.punchline: Charlie's completely unconcerned 'Probably' to whether the pies contain actual turtle
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — one word does the work. 'Probably' as a response to 'are they made from real turtle' is exactly right. It acknowledges the possibility without caring. Very quotable and captures the show's dark humor perfectly.

jokes.text: Mac's lips — 'mine are for sale' about TMNT pies / Charlie: 'He has a very minimal share, Frank'
jokes.setup: Frank wants to buy the pies; Charlie says they're not for sale; Mac immediately offers to sell his share
jokes.punchline: Mac tries to independently sell his fraction of the investment the moment there's a buyer; Charlie quickly minimizes his share as 'very minimal'
jokes.explanation: Good dynamic beat about Mac's immediate self-interest vs. Charlie controlling the terms of the deal. 'He has a very minimal share, Frank' as a negotiating move is sharp.

jokes.text: Charlie leverages supply/demand: 'Not when your demand is more than the supply' — Charlie walks Frank through his own financial lesson back at him
jokes.setup: Frank says the market dictates value; Charlie refuses
jokes.punchline: Charlie uses Frank's own opening inflation lecture — specifically the supply/demand lesson — to justify his pricing power
jokes.explanation: Charlie using Frank's own first-scene economics lecture to outmaneuver him in a negotiation is structurally excellent. It validates the episode's opening scene — the inflation tutorial wasn't just a cold open joke, it was setting up Charlie's endgame. Frank being bested by his own lesson is perfect. The character integration is high: Charlie has absorbed exactly the lesson he needed and ignored everything else. This is one of the episode's strongest structural moments.

jokes.text: Charlie has bought 'the last remaining ones there are' — cornered the entire market in TMNT Pies
jokes.setup: Frank says he'll get the pies somewhere else
jokes.punchline: Charlie has bought every remaining TMNT pie in existence — his obsessive investment extends to cornering the market
jokes.explanation: Great escalation. Charlie didn't just buy some pies — he executed a genuine market cornering strategy (accidentally or intentionally). The reveal shifts Charlie from buffoon to savant, which is a great Always Sunny move. The earlier dismissals of Charlie's business acumen make this landing even more satisfying.

jokes.text: 'And you kept it crypto.' — Dennis uses Charlie's earlier malapropism as a compliment
jokes.setup: Charlie has cornered the market on TMNT pies
jokes.punchline: 'You kept it crypto' — using Charlie's earlier confusion between 'crypto' and 'cryptic' as a sincere compliment for his secretive strategy
jokes.explanation: Among the best moments in the episode and arguably the most elegantly constructed joke. Dennis unintentionally validates Charlie's malapropism by using it correctly — 'kept it crypto' means both 'kept it secret' (cryptic) AND aligns with the episode's crypto/investment theme. It retroactively makes Charlie's verbal mistake into sophisticated foreshadowing. The payoff is proportional to how early the setup was planted. Economy is near-perfect — four words close a loop that was opened 15 minutes earlier. This approaches top-tier Always Sunny writing.

jokes.text: Charlie's terms to Frank: board up the new room AND the noisy toilet, forgive the loan, give Dee her apartment back — 'return everything to the status quo'
jokes.setup: Charlie has Frank over a barrel and can name his price
jokes.punchline: His demands include boarding up the room AND the toilet he was hiding — actively reducing his apartment back to its previous squalid state — and 'return everything to the status quo'
jokes.explanation: This is Charlie's most Charlie moment. Having won, he uses his leverage to restore his apartment to its worse previous state — specifically asking that the toilet be boarded back up and the room hidden again. His ideal living situation involves pissing in cans and sleeping with Frank. The phrase 'return everything to the status quo' as Charlie's demand when holding all the cards is both deeply funny and oddly poignant about the show's reset-button nature. High character integration: no other character on television would use power to decrease their quality of life. The fact that he includes Dee's apartment (genuine altruism) alongside 'board up my toilet' (genuine insanity) makes it perfect.

jokes.text: Charlie's terms for selling the pies: board up the new room, forgive the loan, give Dee her apartment back — 'return everything to the status quo'
jokes.setup: Frank wants to buy the pies; Charlie names his price
jokes.punchline: 'Return everything to the status quo' — Charlie's ultimate ambition is to get back to the exact terrible situation they were in at the start
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Charlie's character and the show's resetting structure. After all the chaos, Charlie's greatest ambition is to restore the exact conditions (pissing in cans, sleeping with Frank, Dee in her apartment) that existed before. 'Return everything to the status quo' as the ultimate prize is both darkly funny and philosophically true to Always Sunny's premise.

jokes.text: Mac is still eating the nuts — Dennis asks if he wants to go to the hospital or Costco; Mac wants Costco
jokes.setup: Mac has had a clear allergic reaction all episode; they're discussing his health
jokes.punchline: Given the choice between medical care and more nuts, Mac chooses more nuts
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff for the episode's coda. Mac choosing Costco over the hospital is consistent with his self-destructive character. Functional final beat.

jokes.text: 'You know what, buddy? I think we'll take you to the hospital, and they'll have nuts, and you can...you can die there.'
jokes.setup: Mac wants to go to Costco instead of the hospital
jokes.punchline: Dennis offers the compromise that the hospital will have nuts — then concludes '...you can die there' with chilling calm
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing line. Dennis begins with gentle accommodation ('they'll have nuts') before pivoting to '...you can die there' — delivered with complete flatness. The pause before 'you can die there' is essential to the rhythm. This is Dennis at his most sociopathic-but-casual, which is the show's hallmark. Strong economy in the construction: the promise of nuts briefly makes it sound kind before the dark pivot.

jokes.text: Mac's condition worsening: 'Does he want to get to the hospital or to Costco?' / 'He wants more nuts.'
jokes.setup: Mac is now clearly in serious medical distress from nut allergy
jokes.punchline: Given the choice between hospital and Costco (more nuts), it's clear Mac would choose Costco; Dennis and Charlie laugh about it
jokes.explanation: Perfect dark ending. 'He wants more nuts' is a great final beat — Mac would choose the thing killing him over medical care. Charlie and Dennis finding this funny rather than alarming is exactly the show's dark comedic register.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'You know what, buddy? I think we'll take you to the hospital, and they'll have nuts, and you can... you can die there.'
jokes.setup: Mac wants to go to Costco instead of the hospital
jokes.punchline: Dennis offers a compromise: the hospital might have nuts there, so Mac can die while eating them
jokes.explanation: A great closing line. Dennis's 'compromise' — going to the hospital because they might have nuts there, 'and you can... you can die there' — is delivered with the right amount of pause before 'die there.' The ellipsis before the punchline is doing real work. It's simultaneously caring (taking Mac to the hospital) and completely indifferent (fine if he dies). This is the show's ethos in one sentence and a very good closer.

tmdb_overview: Dennis and Mac get into inflatable furniture to deal with the economy’s inflation, while Dee tries to find a place to crash after being evicted by her greedy landlord and Charlie wants to pitch Frank his crypto/online investment idea. And in this inflation episode everything gets bigger - Dee’s desperation, Mac’s lips, and even Charlie’s apartment!
